source_claims.claim: Docker packages software in lightweight containers using OS-level virtualization and automates deployment across environments.
Docker originated as a dotCloud internal project, debuted publicly in 2013, used LXC initially, then moved to libcontainer and later created Moby.
Docker adoption expanded through Red Hat, Microsoft, AWS, IBM, Oracle, Windows/WSL2, Docker Desktop licensing, AtomicJar, and major 2025 releases.
Docker uses Linux kernel interfaces, namespaces, cgroups and union-capable filesystems; macOS uses a Linux VM.
Docker software architecture includes dockerd, Docker CLI, Docker objects, registries and Dockerfiles.
Dockerfile example uses ARG, FROM, COPY, ENV, RUN, VOLUME and EXPOSE.
Docker Compose defines/runs multi-container applications and Docker Swarm provides clustering and Raft consensus.
Docker Volumes provide independent persistence and licensing differs between Docker Engine and Docker Desktop.
Related technologies include Linux, DevOps, gVisor, Kubernetes, microservices, OCI and related software architecture.

value.name: Cryptographic hash function
value.definition: A deterministic algorithm that maps an arbitrary-length binary input to a fixed-length digest, with security goals including preimage resistance, second-preimage resistance, and collision resistance.

value.primary_source: User-supplied Wikipedia article text: Cryptographic hash function
value.scope_note: The graph follows the supplied article's terminology and coverage, while adding explicit relationship structure, schema, patterns, and cautious engineering rules for machine use.
source_derived_content: Merkle–Damgård, wide-pipe, sponge, and HAIFA constructions
value.editorial_caveat: Algorithm status and parameter recommendations change. Use current standards and expert review for production decisions; the graph is not a substitute for a cryptographic design review.

value.name: Secure file verification
value.purpose: Detect modification or substitution of downloaded content.
steps: Obtain the expected digest from an authenticated/trusted source.
Compute the digest of the received file with a suitable modern algorithm.
Compare values using the correct algorithm and encoding.
If a mismatch occurs, reject or investigate the file; if it matches, interpret the result only within the trust model.
caveats: A digest posted beside a file on the same unauthenticated channel may be replaced together with the file.
A matching hash does not prove that software is benign or that the publisher is trustworthy.

value.name: Password storage with a password KDF
value.purpose: Reduce the rate of offline password guessing after a verifier database is exposed.
steps: Generate a unique random salt per password.
Derive a verifier using a password KDF such as Argon2, scrypt, bcrypt, or PBKDF2 with appropriate parameters.
Store the algorithm identifier, parameters, salt, and verifier.
On login, recompute and compare; upgrade parameters as policy changes.
caveats: Do not store plaintext passwords.
Do not use a fast hash such as raw SHA-256 or SHA-1 alone for password storage.
Parameter choices should follow current platform and standards guidance.

value.name: HMAC message authentication
value.purpose: Authenticate messages using a shared secret and a standardized keyed construction.
steps: Agree on a secure hash and shared secret key.
Compute the HMAC over the canonical message representation.
Transmit the message and authentication tag.
Receiver recomputes the HMAC and compares tags using an appropriate constant-time comparison.
caveats: Do not substitute naive hash(secret || message) constructions for HMAC.
Key management and message canonicalization remain important.

value.name: Content-addressed storage
value.purpose: Address and deduplicate objects based on content.
steps: Select a collision-resistant hash and a canonical byte representation.
Hash the content to derive a content address.
Store the object and index its address to physical storage.
On retrieval, recompute the hash to verify content integrity.
caveats: Collision handling and algorithm migration should be part of the design.
The content address is not automatically a claim of publisher authenticity.

value.name: Merkle-tree verification
value.purpose: Commit to a large data set and verify components using a root digest and authentication path.
steps: Hash each leaf using an unambiguous encoding.
Hash internal nodes from their child hashes.
Publish or authenticate the root digest.
Verify a selected leaf by recomputing its path to the root.
caveats: Tree layout, leaf/node domain separation, and encoding must be specified to avoid ambiguity.

value.name: Hash-based proof of work
value.purpose: Make request creation moderately costly while allowing cheap validation.
steps: Define a target predicate over a hash output.
Vary a nonce or candidate header and compute hashes until the predicate passes.
Send the candidate and proof.
Verifier performs one or a small number of hash computations and checks the predicate.
caveats: Difficulty must be calibrated; proof of work does not itself establish the truth or legitimacy of the submitted content.

value.name: Cryptographic hash algorithm migration
value.purpose: Retire weak digest algorithms while maintaining interoperability.
steps: Inventory every algorithm use and stored identifier format.
Choose a modern algorithm appropriate to the use case and threat model.
Version formats and APIs so algorithm identity is explicit.
Where feasible, verify old objects and add new digests; plan dual-read or staged migration.
Monitor standards and cryptanalysis and retire obsolete formats.
caveats: A digest's byte length alone does not uniquely identify the algorithm.
Do not assume legacy digests become secure because they are combined with a modern digest.

value.statement: A cryptographic hash is not encryption and has no decryption key or general inverse operation.
A matching digest proves only a content match relative to the expected digest and trust chain; it does not establish that the content is safe or benign.
For an ideal n-bit hash, generic preimage work is about 2^n and generic collision work about 2^(n/2); real algorithms may be weaker due to cryptanalysis.
Fast general-purpose hashes should not be used alone to store passwords; use a salted password KDF with current recommended parameters.
For hash-based message authentication, use HMAC or another reviewed construction rather than naive secret-prefix/suffix hashing.
MD5 and SHA-1 are unsuitable for new applications that depend on collision resistance.
CRC-32 and similar checksums detect accidental corruption but do not provide cryptographic protection against intentional manipulation.
Persist the algorithm name/version and output parameters alongside a digest; digest bytes alone are not a robust self-describing identifier.

value.title: File digest comparison
value.input: A downloaded archive and a trusted SHA-256 digest string.
steps: Compute SHA-256 over the exact downloaded bytes.
Encode the result consistently, commonly as hexadecimal.
Compare with the authenticated expected digest.
value.output: Equal digests provide strong evidence of byte-for-byte identity under SHA-256's security assumptions and the trust model.

value.title: Leading-zero proof of work
value.input: A candidate message/header plus a nonce.
steps: Hash the candidate.
Check whether the digest begins with the required number of zero bits.
If not, vary the nonce and repeat.
value.output: A valid candidate is relatively cheap to verify; expected search effort grows exponentially with the number of required leading zero bits.

value.title: Digest commitment
value.input: A secret solution m held by Alice.
steps: Alice computes H(m) and publishes the digest before revealing m.
Bob later computes H(m) over the revealed solution.
They compare the result to the earlier commitment.
value.output: The matching digest supports the claim that the revealed solution matches the committed value, assuming the hash and protocol are appropriate.

value.title: Salted password verifier
value.input: Password candidate, unique random salt, KDF name and parameters.
steps: Derive a verifier with the selected password KDF.
Store the salt, algorithm parameters and verifier, not the plaintext password.
At login, derive again and compare.
value.output: Unique salts reduce cross-account precomputation and KDF cost slows each password guess.

examples.input: A candidate message/header plus a nonce.
steps: Hash the candidate.
Check whether the digest begins with the required number of zero bits.
If not, vary the nonce and repeat.
examples.output: A valid candidate is relatively cheap to verify; expected search effort grows exponentially with the number of required leading zero bits.

examples.title: Digest commitment
examples.input: A secret solution m held by Alice.
steps: Alice computes H(m) and publishes the digest before revealing m.
Bob later computes H(m) over the revealed solution.
They compare the result to the earlier commitment.
examples.output: The matching digest supports the claim that the revealed solution matches the committed value, assuming the hash and protocol are appropriate.

examples.title: Salted password verifier
examples.input: Password candidate, unique random salt, KDF name and parameters.
steps: Derive a verifier with the selected password KDF.
Store the salt, algorithm parameters and verifier, not the plaintext password.
At login, derive again and compare.
examples.output: Unique salts reduce cross-account precomputation and KDF cost slows each password guess.

Correlate with current vendor advisories and validated indicators.
Document confidence and false-positive considerations before response.

steps: Isolate the device from untrusted networks.

Rotate credentials and close exposed management/service paths.
Patch, verify, and monitor before returning the device to service.
